lines.text: Bram told it sitting on the garden steps in the snow, looking at the dead roses instead of at me.
I was her steward. Your father brought her here and said, nobody is ever to know she's here, Bram. So nobody ever did.
She never claimed anyone, my lord. Not me, not the village, not a dog. She said that was how they found people like her. So she held it all in.
She only ever claimed two things. Those roses. And you.
She sang to me every night, he said. The same song. Slow and low, like wind going round a chimney.
The night they came, it was snowing. Twelve lenses at the gate. She put you in my arms, wrapped in her own shawl.
Take him out the back, Bram. Over the pass, to his father. And keep him warm.
Keep him warm. The same words she had said to Ash, in the dark under the cathedral, with her hand on his head.
Three days over the pass, in a blizzard. You were so cold, my lord. Hollow-born babies run cold. I didn't know that then.
So I carried you inside my coat, against my chest, with my left arm round you. Three days. I never moved that arm. I was afraid you'd stop breathing.
When he reached Varr Keep, the arm had frozen solid around me. They took it off a week later.
Best trade I ever made.
I looked at his pinned-up sleeve. I'd seen it every day since I came to Greyhollow, and never once asked.
You were worth an arm, my lord. You've been worth a great deal more since. Don't make a fuss.
Then he came back alone, kept her house for fourteen years, and waited. Until a skinny boy with no rings came up the road with a deed in his brother's hand.
Welcome to Greyhollow, my lord. Fourteen years I'd waited to say that. I nearly couldn't get it out.
I couldn't say anything at all. So I did the thing he had taught me. I sat beside him, and was warm.
Three days later, a column came up the south road under black and gold. A thousand Varr levies, with my brother riding at the front.
Father told me everything, the morning the column came. I've had all winter to decide what you are to me, little brother.
And?
You're my little brother. The rest is Father's problem.
His rings flared as he said it. Ember, hot and steady, not the white fire of the draught. Real. His own.
That night, Bram gave me the key to the garden. He didn't say anything. He didn't have to.
The Lord Who Measured Zero. Chapter one hundred and thirty-four, coming soon.
